topic.name: Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $OGHO,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
question.explanation:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

\[ C = \{-C_1\} \cup \{-C_2\} \cup C_3, \]

where $-C_1$ and $-C_2$ are the same paths as $C_1$ and $C_2$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int\limits_{-C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{-C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= -\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} - \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} . \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $DEFD,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the clockwise direction?
question.explanation:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

\[ C = C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \{-C_3\}, \]

where $-C_3$ is the same path as $C_3$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{-C_3} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} - \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} . \end{align*}

example.title: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions

question.text:
The path $C_1$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(0,8)$ to the point $A(-2,8),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a section of the curve $y=-x^3$ from the point $A(-2,8)$ to the point $O(0,0).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 16,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = xy\,\mathbf{i} + y\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
question.explanation:
We will use the fact that \[ \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}. \]

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the section of the curve $y = -x^3$ from $A$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}_2(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} - t^3\,\mathbf{j}, \end{align*} where $-2 \leq t \leq 0.$ Along this curve, we have $x = t$ and $y = -t^3.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_2(t)) & = xy\,\mathbf{i} + y\,\mathbf{j} \\[3pt] & = -t^4\,\mathbf{i} - t^3\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing the derivative, we get the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_2(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( -t^3 \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{i} - 3t^2\,\mathbf{j} \end{align*}

We can now compute the dot product: \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_2(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'_2(t) &= \big( -t^4\,\mathbf{i} - t^3\,\mathbf{j} \big) \cdot \big( \mathbf{i} - 3t^2\,\mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &= -t^4+3t^5 \end{align*}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: \begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} & = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}\\[5pt] & = 16 + \int_{-2}^{0} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r_2}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'_2(t) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = 16 + \int_{-2}^{0} (-t^4+3t^5) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 16 + \left[ -\dfrac{1}{5}t^5 + \dfrac{1}{2}t^6 \right]_{-2}^0 \\[5pt] & = 16 + \left[0 -\left( -\dfrac{(-2^5)}{5} + \dfrac{(-2)^6}{2}\right) \right] \\[5pt] &= 16 - \dfrac{192}{5} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{112}{5} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves

question.text: Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = 4 \, \mathbf{i} + xz \, \mathbf{j} + y \, \mathbf{k}$ and let $C$ be a path in $\mathbb R^3.$ Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}?$
question.explanation:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field \[ \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + Q(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + R(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \] defined on $C,$ we have

\[ \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z) \, \text{d}x + Q(x,y,z) \, \text{d}y + R(x,y,z) \, \text{d}z. \]

Therefore, in our case, we obtain \begin{align} \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & = \int\limits_C 4 \, \text{d}x + xz \, \text{d}y + y \, \text{d}z. \end{align}

example.title: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields

question.text: If $\displaystyle\int\limits_C (y-z) \, \textrm dx + 6z^2 \, \textrm d y - 4y \,\textrm d z $ is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r$ for some piecewise smooth curve $C,$ then $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = $
question.explanation:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field \[ \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + Q(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + R(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \] defined on $C,$ we have \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_C P \, \text{d}x + Q \, \text{d}y + R \, \text{d}z \]

In our case, $P = y-z, Q = 6z^2, R = -4y.$ Therefore

\begin{align} \int\limits_C \left( (y-z) \, \mathbf i + 6z^2 \, \mathbf j - 4y \, \mathbf k\right) \cdot \text{d}\mathbf r & = \displaystyle\int\limits_C (y-z) \, \textrm dx + 6z^2 \, \textrm d y - 4y \, \textrm d z . \end{align}

So, $\mathbf F = (y-z) \, \mathbf i + 6z^2 \, \mathbf j - 4y \, \mathbf k.$
